name: Swarna Kaleeswarar Temple, Kalayarkoil (Thirukkanapper)
deity: Shiva as Swarna Kaleeswarar, with the goddess Swarnavalli; also Someswarar and Sundareswarar
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Pandya Nadu, sung by Sambandar and Sundarar in the Tevaram (7th–8th century)
dynasty: Pandya country; renovated by the Marudhu brothers of Sivaganga (18th century)
summary: At Kalayarkoil in Sivaganga district, three Shiva shrines stand within one great temple beneath a soaring gopuram raised by the Marudhu brothers: the Thirukkanapper of the Tevaram.

sections.history: Kalayarkoil is old even by Tamil reckoning. As Kaanapper it appears in a Purananuru poem of the Sangam age, and as Thirukkanapper it was sung in the Tevaram by Sambandar and Sundarar, making it one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and one of the fourteen in Pandya Nadu. The temple grew over many centuries, but the name most tied to it is that of the Marudhu brothers, Periya Marudhu and Chinna Marudhu, who ruled Sivaganga in the late eighteenth century. They renovated the shrine and raised its towering gopuram, and Kalayarkoil was also a stronghold in their resistance to the East India Company. Their memorial stands across the street from the temple, which is still cared for by the Sivaganga devasthanam.
sections.architecture: The complex is unusual in holding three principal shrines side by side: Swarna Kaleeswarar with the goddess Swarnavalli at the centre, Someswarar with Soundaravalli, and Sundareswarar with Meenakshi. Two gopurams mark the entrance, the taller of nine tiers rising some 150 feet, among the loftiest in southern Tamil Nadu; tradition says the gopuram of the Meenakshi temple at Madurai could be seen from its top. Beside the temple lies the great tank known as the Aanai Madu, the elephant's pool, with a mandapam at its centre.
sections.legends: The village takes its name from a story of Sundarar. Arriving here, the saint saw that the ground was thick with hidden lingams and would not set foot on it for fear of treading on the Lord. Shiva then appeared as a bull, a kaalai, and led him by a path that held no lingam beneath it — so the place became Kalaiyar Kovil, the temple of the Lord who came as a bull. Tradition also holds that the Aanai Madu tank was dug by Airavata, the white elephant of Indra.
sections.festivals: Two festivals lead the year: the Thai Poosam car festival of Swarna Kaleeswarar in January–February and the Vaikasi Visakam brahmotsavam of Someswarar in May–June. Aadi Pooram is kept for the goddess Swarnavalli, Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed, and the Marudhu brothers are remembered at their guru puja each October; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: The gopuram is visible long before the town appears, rising above the plain of Sivaganga. Inside, devotees move from shrine to shrine to worship all three forms of the Lord and their consorts, then walk out to the wide Aanai Madu tank. Pausing at the Marudhu brothers' memorial completes a visit that is as much about Tamil history as about devotion.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most temples of the region. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctums; in the outer corridors and around the tank, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Kalayarkoil is about 18 km east of Sivaganga and roughly 65 km from Madurai by road, with regular buses from both. Sivaganga has the nearest railway station, and Madurai Airport is the nearest airport.
